title: Out-of-Bag (OOB) Evaluation
abstract:
Bootstrap sampling leaves roughly 37% of the rows unseen by each model. Those
out-of-bag rows are, for that model, genuine held-out data — so a bagging
ensemble can validate itself for free, with no train/validation split at all.
This document covers the mechanism, the derivation of the 37% figure, why OOB is
slightly pessimistic, how it compares with $k$-fold cross-validation in accuracy
and cost, the situations in which it is unreliable, and how to use it for
hyperparameter tuning.

blocks.t: Where 37% Comes From
The derivation

A bootstrap sample draws $n$ rows from $n$ with replacement. For a
particular row, the chance of not being picked on any single draw is
$1-\frac1n$, and the draws are independent, so
P(\text{row never drawn})=\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n}.
Using $\left(1+\frac{x}{n}\right)^{n}\to e^{x}$,
\boxed{ \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n}=e^{-1}\approx0.368 }

So each model trains on about 63% of the distinct rows and about
37% are out-of-bag for it. The convergence is fast — already
$0.366$ at $n=100$ — so the figure holds for any realistic dataset.
Why this is a legitimate validation set

For tree $b$, the out-of-bag rows are data that tree never saw during
fitting. Its predictions on them are therefore genuine held-out predictions.
Repeat over all $B$ trees and every row has been held out by roughly $37\%$ of
them, so every row gets an honest prediction — from a sub-ensemble of about
$0.37B$ trees.

Every row is used for training and for evaluation, without ever
splitting the data. That is what the notes mean by "no need of validation
data".
The OOB score

\hat y_i^{\text{oob}}
 =\operatorname{aggregate}\Big{\hat f_b(x_i) : i\notin \text{bag}(b)\Big},
 \qquad
 \text{OOB score}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{1} \left[\hat y_i^{\text{oob}}=y_i\right]
— majority vote for classification, mean for regression.
OOB vs Cross-Validation

blocks.t: Why OOB is slightly pessimistic

Each OOB prediction is made by only about $37\%$ of the trees, so it comes from a
smaller ensemble than the one you will actually deploy. A smaller ensemble
has higher variance and is therefore slightly worse. With 500 trees the OOB
prediction still uses $\approx185$, so the gap is negligible; with 20 trees it
uses $\approx7$ and OOB can understate the model noticeably. Use enough
trees before trusting the OOB score.
Where OOB is unreliable

items:
bootstrap=False. No sampling means no out-of-bag rows and
 scikit-learn raises an error.

Too few estimators. Some rows may be in-bag for every tree, so
 they get no OOB prediction at all — sklearn warns about this.

Preprocessing outside the model. If you scaled or imputed on the
 full dataset before fitting, the OOB rows were already contaminated. OOB
 cannot detect leakage the way a properly constructed pipeline plus CV can
 (Topic 17).

Grouped or temporal data. OOB assumes rows are exchangeable. With
 repeated measurements per customer or a time ordering, a near-duplicate of
 an OOB row is almost certainly in-bag, and OOB becomes optimistic. Use
 GroupKFold or TimeSeriesSplit instead.

blocks.t: Using It for Tuning

The notes' final point — helps hyperparameter tuning without splitting the
data — is its main practical use. Fit once per candidate configuration and read
oob_score_, instead of fitting $k$ times per candidate. On a grid of $G$
configurations that is $G$ fits rather than $kG$, a five-fold saving.
The one place OOB is genuinely irreplaceable

On a small dataset, holding out 20% for validation is expensive — you lose a
fifth of your training signal. OOB lets you train on 100% of the rows and still
obtain an honest estimate. That combination is not available from any other
method.
Code

import numpy as np, time, warnings
from sklearn.ensemble import (RandomForestClassifier, RandomForestRegressor,
                              BaggingClassifier)
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 3000
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 12))
y = (1.8*X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] - .7*X[:, 2] + .5*X[:, 0]*X[:, 1]
     + rng.normal(0, 1.1, n) > 0).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25,
                                          stratify=y, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE 37% FIGURE
# =====================================================================
print(f"{'n':>7s} {'measured OOB fraction':>22s} {'(1-1/n)^n':>12s}")
for n_ in [10, 50, 100, 1000, 10_000]:
    frac = np.mean([1 - len(set(np.random.default_rng(s).integers(0, n_, n_)))/n_
                    for s in range(300)])
    print(f"{n_:7d} {frac:22.4f} {(1-1/n_)**n_:12.4f}")
print(f"{'limit':>7s} {1/np.e:22.4f} {'1/e':>12s}")

# =====================================================================
# 2. OOB FROM SCRATCH -- aggregate only the trees that never saw the row
# =====================================================================
def manual_oob(X, y, B=200, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    votes = np.zeros((len(X), 2))
    counted = np.zeros(len(X), int)
    for b in range(B):
        idx = r.integers(0, len(X), len(X))               # bootstrap
        oob = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(X)), idx)        # rows NOT in the bag
        m = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=b).fit(X[idx], y[idx])
        p = m.predict(X[oob])
        votes[oob, p] += 1                                # only OOB rows vote
        counted[oob] += 1
    scored = counted > 0
    pred = votes[scored].argmax(axis=1)
    return accuracy_score(y[scored], pred), counted

score, counted = manual_oob(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\nscratch OOB accuracy: {score:.4f}")
print(f"rows with at least one OOB prediction: {(counted>0).mean():.4%}")
print(f"average trees per OOB prediction: {counted.mean():.1f} of 200 "
      f"({counted.mean()/200:.1%} -- close to 1/e)")

# =====================================================================
# 3. SKLEARN'S VERSION -- one extra argument
# =====================================================================
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, oob_score=True,
                            random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\nOOB score      : {rf.oob_score_:.4f}")
print(f"true test score: {rf.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"5-fold CV score: "
      f"{cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1), X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, n_jobs=-1).mean():.4f}")
print(f"training score : {rf.score(X_tr, y_tr):.4f}   <- meaningless, it memorised")

# The raw OOB decision function is available too:
print(f"\noob_decision_function_ shape: {rf.oob_decision_function_.shape}")
print("manual accuracy from it:",
      round(accuracy_score(y_tr, rf.oob_decision_function_.argmax(1)), 4))

# =====================================================================
# 4. OOB IS PESSIMISTIC WITH FEW TREES
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'n_estimators':>13s} {'OOB':>8s} {'test':>8s} {'gap':>8s} "
      f"{'trees per OOB pred':>20s}")
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    for B in [5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 300, 1000]:
        m = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=B, oob_score=True,
                                   random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
        print(f"{B:13d} {m.oob_score_:8.4f} {m.score(X_te, y_te):8.4f} "
              f"{m.score(X_te,y_te)-m.oob_score_:8.4f} {B/np.e:20.1f}")
# With 5 trees each OOB prediction comes from ~2 trees -- a far weaker
# ensemble than the one you deploy, so OOB understates it.

# =====================================================================
# 5. TUNING WITH OOB -- one fit per candidate instead of k
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'max_features':>13s} {'OOB score':>11s}")
best, best_mf = -1, None
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for mf in [1, 2, "sqrt", "log2", 6, None]:
    m = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, max_features=mf,
                               oob_score=True, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{str(mf):>13s} {m.oob_score_:11.4f}")
    if m.oob_score_ > best:
        best, best_mf = m.oob_score_, mf
t_oob = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"best by OOB: max_features={best_mf}  ({t_oob:.1f}s for 6 fits)")

t0 = time.perf_counter()
gs = GridSearchCV(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
                  {"max_features": [1, 2, "sqrt", "log2", 6, None]},
                  cv=5, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
t_cv = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"best by 5-fold CV: max_features={gs.best_params_['max_features']}  "
      f"({t_cv:.1f}s for 30 fits)")
print(f"OOB was {t_cv/t_oob:.1f}x faster and agreed: "
      f"{best_mf == gs.best_params_['max_features']}")

# =====================================================================
# 6. WHERE OOB FAILS
# =====================================================================
try:
    RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, bootstrap=False,
                           oob_score=True).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
except Exception as e:
    print(f"\nbootstrap=False: {type(e).__name__} -- no sampling, no OOB rows")

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=3, oob_score=True,
                           random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    if w: print(f"too few trees: {str(w[0].message)[:70]}")

# GROUPED DATA -- OOB becomes OPTIMISTIC
groups = rng.integers(0, 300, len(X_tr))           # 10 rows per customer
Xg = X_tr + rng.normal(0, .05, X_tr.shape)         # near-duplicates within a group
Xg = Xg[np.argsort(groups)]; yg = y_tr[np.argsort(groups)]
m = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, oob_score=True,
                           random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(Xg, yg)
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold
gk = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
                     Xg, yg, groups=np.sort(groups), cv=GroupKFold(5), n_jobs=-1).mean()
print(f"\ngrouped data: OOB {m.oob_score_:.4f}   GroupKFold {gk:.4f}")
print("OOB is OPTIMISTIC -- a near-duplicate of every OOB row is in-bag.")

# =====================================================================
# 7. WHERE OOB IS IRREPLACEABLE -- small datasets
# =====================================================================
Xs, ys = X[:150], y[:150]
Xs_tr, Xs_val, ys_tr, ys_val = train_test_split(Xs, ys, test_size=.2, random_state=0)

holdout = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0,
                                 n_jobs=-1).fit(Xs_tr, ys_tr)
full = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, oob_score=True,
                              random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(Xs, ys)
print(f"\nsmall dataset (150 rows):")
print(f"  holdout: trained on {len(ys_tr)} rows, validated on {len(ys_val)}")
print(f"           validation score {holdout.score(Xs_val, ys_val):.4f}")
print(f"  OOB    : trained on ALL {len(ys)} rows")
print(f"           OOB score {full.oob_score_:.4f}")
# OOB uses 100% of the data for training AND still gives an honest estimate.

# =====================================================================
# 8. IT WORKS FOR REGRESSION AND FOR PLAIN BAGGING TOO
# =====================================================================
yr = X[:, 0]*2 + X[:, 1] - .5*X[:, 2]**2 + rng.normal(0, 1, n)
rfr = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, oob_score=True,
                            random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X[:2000], yr[:2000])
print(f"\nregressor OOB R2 {rfr.oob_score_:.4f}   "
      f"test R2 {rfr.score(X[2000:], yr[2000:]):.4f}")

bag = BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=300,
                        oob_score=True, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"BaggingClassifier OOB {bag.oob_score_:.4f}  test {bag.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
# Any bootstrap-based ensemble can do this -- it is a property of bagging,
# not of random forests specifically.
Worked Examples
Out-of-bag prediction for one row
Dataset of $n=10$ rows, forest of $B=3$ bootstrap trees. Each tree is trained on its own bootstrap sample.
Step 1 – which trees did not see row 7? Suppose row 7 was absent from the bootstrap samples of trees 1 and 3, but present in tree 2.

Step 2 – the OOB prediction. Only trees 1 and 3 may predict row 7. If they vote $[\text{class }1,\;\text{class }0]$ (a tie), the OOB rule breaks it by the standard convention or by averaged probability. Crucially, row 7 is never scored by a tree that trained on it.

Step 3 – how many rows are OOB for a tree? For $n=10$ each row is left out with probability $0.349$, so about 3.5 of the 10 rows are OOB for each tree. With large $n$ this tends to $0.368$ (that is $1/e$).

Step 4 – the OOB score. Repeat for all rows, compare each OOB prediction with its true label, and aggregate. This gives a validation estimate with no separate hold-out set, at the cost of each row being scored by only about a third of the trees.
Summary
Everything on one page

While sampling data with repetition, about 37% of the data is
 never sent to any given model in bagging — because
 $(1-1/n)^n\to e^{-1}\approx0.368$.

Those rows can be used as a validation set, as the model has
 never seen them.

For each row, aggregate only the trees that never saw it. Every row is
 used for training and for evaluation.

Thus no need of validation data, and it helps
 hyperparameter tuning without splitting the data — one fit per
 candidate instead of $k$.

OOB is slightly pessimistic, because each OOB prediction comes
 from only $\approx37\%$ of the trees. Use enough estimators before
 trusting it.

It fails when bootstrap=False, when there are too few trees, when
 preprocessing leaked before fitting, and on grouped or temporal
 data, where it becomes optimistic.

It is irreplaceable on small datasets: train on 100% of the rows
 and still get an honest estimate.

It works for regression and for plain bagging too — it is a property of

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. What is out-of-bag evaluation?

Bootstrap sampling leaves about 37% of the rows unseen by each tree. For each
row, aggregate only the trees that never saw it — those predictions are genuine
held-out predictions, so the ensemble validates itself without any train/validation
split.
Q. Where does 37% come from?

The probability a given row is never drawn in $n$ draws with replacement is
$(1-1/n)^n$, which converges to $e^{-1}\approx0.368$. It is already $0.366$ at
$n=100$, so the figure holds for any realistic dataset.
Q. OOB or cross-validation?

OOB when you are using a bagging ensemble and want a fast estimate — one fit
instead of $k$, and all the data used for training. Cross-validation when you need
to compare across model families, when preprocessing must be inside the fold to
prevent leakage, or when the data is grouped or temporal.
Q. Why is the OOB score usually a little below the test score?

Because each OOB prediction is made by only about a third of the trees, so it
comes from a smaller and therefore higher-variance ensemble than the one you
deploy. With hundreds of trees the gap is negligible; with a handful it is not.
Q. When is OOB misleading?

With grouped or temporal data. OOB assumes rows are exchangeable, so if a customer
appears ten times, a near-duplicate of every out-of-bag row is almost certainly
in-bag and the estimate becomes optimistic. Use GroupKFold or
TimeSeriesSplit there.
Q. Can OOB replace the test set entirely?

For model selection and tuning, largely yes. For the final reported number, keep a
genuine held-out test set — once you have selected max_features by OOB
score, that OOB score has been used for selection and is no longer an unbiased
estimate, exactly as with any validation set (Topic 07).
